title: Sick on a journey
hookLine: Basho's last poem: sick on a journey, dreams wander withered fields (1694)
tomorrow: Issa lost his little girl. what two words did his poem end on?
last: MOMENTS · UNDER THE TREES · WHAT I HAVE SEEN.

cards: A trip cut short has its own ache: the fever on the last morning, the ride home early, the trail map with the end still unmarked. Basho's final journey ended something like that.
In Osaka, far from his home, he fell ill, and his students gathered around his bed. From that bed came the poem remembered as his last: tabi ni yande, yume wa kareno wo, kakemeguru.
Sick on a journey, my dreams go wandering over withered fields.

teach.b: Notice the season word, even here: kareno, withered fields, a winter word. The body lies in bed. The dreams are still out walking, over winter fields.

teach.h: EVERY POEM COULD BE THE LAST.
teach.b: A story his students told says that when someone asked him for a farewell poem, a custom among Japanese poets, he answered that any of his poems could be his last, because he had written each one as if it were.
Here's the teaching, and it gathers up the whole week. Read with the Zen eye this week has followed, a journey isn't measured by whether it reaches the end.
Each step was the road. Each poem was complete when it was written. Basho didn't finish wandering.
His last poem doesn't mourn the unfinished road. It makes a poem of it, with the season in it. Now look back over the week.
The butterfly that has time enough in moments. The school under the trees. Tagore's parting word of thanks.
The season word that pins a moment as it passes. The summer grasses over the warriors' dreams. The road that was itself the home.
Again and again this week, two poets made something whole out of what was brief, or broken off. So the trip that ended early, the plan that never got its last day, still counts as the road.
Dreams wander, even over winter fields.

how: Basho's last poem is read on the anniversary of his death, kept in Japan as a haiku memorial day in early winter; haiku poets sometimes write a farewell poem, or let their last poem stand as one.

games.q: what does “sick on a journey” mean?
o: dreams still wandering while the body lies ill
a fever dream that frightens a traveler
planning tomorrow's walk before you sleep

games.q: the last stretch of the road: tap the pairs.
p: where Basho fell ill on his last journey
withered fields: a winter season word
what his students asked him for
still wandering while the body rests

s: Basho wrote his last poem at home, in his own hut
he fell ill on a journey, in Osaka, with his students around him.
withered fields is a winter season word
kareno: even the last poem carries a kigo.
in haiku's Zen-shaped view, an unfinished journey is a failed one
each step was the road. Basho made his unfinished journey into a poem.

games.q: a friend's father died before finishing the book he was writing. she wonders whether to throw the versions away. what fits Basho's last poem?
o: keep them: an unfinished journey isn't wasted, and his dreams are in them.
throw them out: a book that was never finished never really counted.
hire someone to finish it quickly, so it can finally count.
games.why: sick on a journey, Basho wrote that his dreams went wandering over withered fields. the unfinished road was still the road.

practice: Bring to mind one journey of yours that didn't finish: a trip, a plan, a visit you meant to make.
Close your eyes and let your thoughts wander over it the way Basho's dreams wandered over the fields, without judging where it stopped. If you like, thank it for the part you walked.
